hops.afterHeading: Two ways to make sisters differ
hops.title: A bacterium that never splits into twins
hops.text: Many people picture bacteria pinching into identical twins. The aquatic *Caulobacter crescentus* never does. Every division yields two different daughters: a stalked cell, which sticks to surfaces with a pad called the holdfast, and a swimmer with a flagellum that can colonize a new surface. Pulling single cells off glass gave an estimated bond strength above 68 newtons per square millimetre at the centre of contact, the strongest biological adhesive the team knew of in 2006. Polar kinases keep the regulator CtrA active in the swimmer, where it silences the replication origin, so only the stalked sister can copy its DNA right away.

sources.citation: Tsang et al., Adhesion of single bacterial cells in the micronewton range, PNAS 103(15):5764-5768 (2006)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A tiny curved bacterium glued to an underwater pebble by a stalk while its tailed sister swims away.
image.caption: Attached Caulobacter makes a stalked daughter that stays and can divide, and a swimmer that can disperse or settle nearby.

hops.title: Elisabeth Gateff and the giant larvae
hops.text: In the 1950s Elisabeth Gateff was declared an enemy of Bulgaria and barred from higher education. She studied in Germany, then joined Howard Schneiderman's group in the United States. There she studied *lethal(2) giant larvae* (*lgl*), a gene first known from a Calvin Bridges mutant. Larvae with two mutant copies carried invasive, lethal brain tumours, and with a transplant method from Ernst Hadorn she passed the tumour cells from adult fly to adult fly an indefinite number of times. That made *lgl* the first tumour suppressor gene shown in animals. Decades later its protein turned up as the helper that aPKC phosphorylates at the top of the neuroblast.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage lab bench with an antique microscope beside a glass fly bottle holding oversized pale larvae.
image.caption: Fly larvae lacking lgl grew transplantable brain tumours, revealing the first tumour suppressor gene found in animals.

hops.title: A human Pins gene and Chudley-McCullough syndrome
hops.text: Mutations in both copies of *GPSM2*, the human relative of fly Pins (LGN in mammals), cause Chudley-McCullough syndrome. Brain scans often show a thin or partly missing corpus callosum, small extra folds in the frontal cortex, and misplaced grey matter. Yet affected people generally have no significant neurodevelopmental problems beyond severe to profound hearing loss. GPSM2 helps orient the spindle, and in 2012 the team linking it to the syndrome proposed that altered divisions might explain the brain changes. In mice it has a second job in inner-ear hair cells: with Gαi, it sits at the tips of the tallest row of stereocilia and helps set their height.

sources.citation: Doherty et al., Am J Hum Genet 90(6):1088-1093 (2012)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Staircase rows of hair-like stereocilia on an inner-ear cell, the tallest row glowing at the tips.
image.caption: GPSM2, a human Pins relative, helps orient spindles; in mice it also marks the tallest stereocilia of ear hair cells.

audio.title: Three Ways Cells Play Favorites
audio.transcript:
Most of us leave introductory biology with a tidy picture of cell division: copy the D N A, split down the middle, get two identical twins. Plenty of living things ignore that picture. Here are three that play favorites.

Start with a bacterium called Caulobacter crescentus, one of the first settlers on surfaces under water. Every time it divides, the two daughters are built for different lives. One daughter has a thin stalk tipped with a sticky pad called the holdfast. If the parent was attached, that daughter stays put. The other is a swarmer with a spinning, corkscrew-shaped flagellum that can swim to a new surface. That holdfast is remarkable. In two thousand six, physicists at Brown University pulled single cells off glass with a micromanipulator. The force averaged about six tenths of a micronewton. Their model put the peak stress at sixty-eight newtons per square millimeter at the center of contact, where the glue meets the glass. Because that interface held, the authors inferred a bond strength above sixty-eight newtons per square millimeter, making it the strongest biological adhesive the team knew of. The difference runs deeper than shape. Kinases parked at the cell's two poles keep a regulator called C t r A active in the swimmer, where it sits on the replication origin and keeps it shut. Only the stalked sister can start copying its D N A right away.

Now to baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Yeast divides by budding, and the bud is not a copy of its mother. Each division leaves a permanent bud scar on the mother's surface, so her surface records how many daughters she has made. Inside her, proteins damaged by oxidation build up as she ages. In two thousand three, a research team in Gothenburg, Sweden, made one kind of protein damage visible in individual cells. They found that this damage tended to stay with the mother as she divided. Mothers lacking a gene called sir two failed to hold the damage back. In normal yeast, newborn daughters started out with much lower levels of this kind of oxidative damage than their mothers, though mothers held it back less well as they aged. Several aging factors are sorted unevenly in parallel, and the shared logic is simple: a division can leave more of some material on one side than the other.

Last, a story about what happens when the sorting machinery breaks. In the nineteen fifties, Elisabeth Gateff was declared an enemy of Bulgaria and barred from higher education. She earned that education in Germany instead, then moved to the United States to join Howard Schneiderman's group and study fruit-fly development. There she studied a gene called lethal two giant larvae, or L G L. Calvin Bridges had isolated the original mutant. Larvae with two broken copies grew invasive, lethal brain tumors. Gateff perfected a method from Ernst Hadorn for transplanting tissue into adult flies, and showed that cells from these tumors could be passed from one fly to the next an indefinite number of times. That made L G L the first tumor suppressor gene found in animals. Decades later, in two thousand three, researchers showed that the kinase a P K C adds phosphate to the L G L protein. They proposed that this happens at the top of a dividing fly neuroblast and helps keep fate-determining cargo at the bottom. The gene Gateff made famous for its tumors turned out to belong to the same sorting machinery.
